newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INSTANT VIEW - Australian retail trade data.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Australian retail trade data.

text.p: Australian retail trade fell 1.8 percent in June, the Bureau of Statistics reported.
Over the June quarter, real retail trade fell 0.5 percent, the data also showed.
Economists' median expectations for the monthly data had centred on a 0.4 percent rise, and ranged from a 1.5 percent fall to a 1.5 percent rise.
For the quarterly data, forecasts centred on a 0.1 percent rise, and ranged from a 0.5 percent fall to a 0.8 percent rise.
A selection of economists' immediate reactions to the data follows.
DAVID DE GARIS, SENIOR TREASURY ECONOMIST, ANZ BANK:

"The numbers are very weak and they do justify the Reserve Bank's action yesterday (to cut official rates). The retail trade numbers are weak and certainly doesn't start off on a stronger note leading into the September quarter, so the near term outlook is still quite subdued for consumer spending."
PETER MUNCKTON, SENIOR ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST:

"They were disappointing. A couple of categories were down very strongly -- department stores and clothing. It's possible with the mid-year sales a little bit later this year that some money from June could be dribbling into July and therefore July could be a bit stronger. The last few months have been all over the place, but it shows consumers are still spending moderately. The consumer overall won't be spending a lot more money until they see more jobs being created and wages in their pockets. After the cut yesterday, it was always likely that the bias was going to be for another easing and this just reaffirms that."
HANS KUNNEN, GROUP ECONOMIST, COLONIAL STATE BANK

"I guess in part they are a reaction to the very strong rise in the previous month, but retail spending is flat. That tells us something about inflation. Retailers, because of the weakness of spending, simply aren't in a position to push up prices. That tells us that the inflation outlook is going to be good going forward and it will set people thinking about the possibility of a rate cut down the track. It's going to be a very flat contribution (to GDP), as obviously it's going to soften the GDP figures. That's going to give us a very mediocre annualised growth rate, within the two percent range."
TONY MEER, ECONOMIST, DEUTSCHE MORGAN GRENFELL:

"Obviously, it was weaker than the market expected and will probably make people focus a bit more on the prospect for further rate cuts by the Reserve Bank which wasn't the consensus before 11.30 (a.m.). In terms of the actual number, I think it would be too much to read into it that spending dropped off so sharply in the month of June. Really it is just a rebound from the previous month's very strong result. If you look at the composition the big falls were in department store sales, clothing and soft goods and what I would suggest there is end of financial year sales which occurred in July this year rather than June. So the seasonal adjustment factor looking for the spending didn't occur but next month will show a quite substantial jump. Where does that leave the trend? -- modest."
STEPHEN ROBERTS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, UBS AUSTRALIA:

"What seems to be happening on the retail side is that people will only spend when there are hints of bargains. So the major sales in May and Jaunary is when we have seen the big spikes in retail trade and it gives up ground very rapidly afterwards. And we have seen this again in the June data. The minus 0.5 percent real for the quarter, even when you allow for slightly firmer vehicle registrations, means consumption spending will be a fairly soft element in GDP."
ANDREW PEASE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, NOMURA:

"Surprisingly weak numbers, they means that retail spending...will make a negative contribution to GDP growth in the June quarter. The spending numbers are puzzling, they're certainly weaker than most people were expecting. The only thing you can say is that the anecdotes seem to be pointing to stronger spending growth. The interest rate cuts at some stage are going to translate to higher spending as well."
NIGEL STAPLEDON, ECONOMIST, WESTPAC BANKING CORP;

"It puts a dampener on relying on the anecdotal evidence, which suggested a mid-year pickup and maybe the July and August numbers will see it looking a bit healthier. This number of itself is pretty inconsequential (for monetary policy). The Reserve Bank is going to give themselves another three months to look at things like employment numbers. There's no question they (this year's weak employment numbers) bought this second round of cuts to the fore. There's also some concern in government circles that business may have been winding back their business investment intentions. The Reserve Bank is right that the economy is coming off such a low base that there is not much risk that by putting their foot down on the accelerator that they're going to put the economy into overdrive. There's not a real risk that in a year or two it's going to be over-heating."
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
